title: Evolution of India's Nuclear Policy

cards.h: From Bhabha's labs to a nuclear triad
cards.b:
India's nuclear story runs from a peaceful energy programme in 1948 to declared weapons in 1998 and a sea-based deterrent today. It shows the pull between idealism (Nehru's call for disarmament) and security (China's 1964 test, Pakistan).

UPSC asks about the phases, the 1974 and 1998 tests, the nuclear doctrine (no first use, credible minimum deterrence) and whether the doctrine still fits after Operation Sindoor (2025).
Scholars call the period from 1974 to 1998 one of 'recessed deterrence' or keeping the option open: India had the capability but did not weaponise openly.

cards.h: Nehru and Bhabha: peaceful atom, open option
cards.b:
Homi J. Bhabha built the programme: the Atomic Energy Commission (1948), the Apsara reactor (1956, Asia's first research reactor) and CIRUS (1960, with Canadian help and US heavy water). He designed the three-stage programme: natural uranium reactors, then fast breeders using plutonium, then thorium, which India has in plenty.

Nehru pressed for a ban on nuclear tests (1954 'standstill' proposal) and for disarmament. But he kept the scientific capacity that could later be used for weapons. After China's test in 1964, Bhabha said India could build a bomb in about 18 months. Shastri approved work on a 'peaceful nuclear explosion' study.

On 18 May 1974, under Indira Gandhi, India tested a device at Pokhran, code-named 'Smiling Buddha'. It called it a peaceful nuclear explosion (PNE).

  • Canada cut nuclear aid, since CIRUS plutonium was used.
  • The Nuclear Suppliers Group (NSG) was set up in 1974–75 to control exports.
  • The US passed the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Act (1978), which ended fuel supply to Tarapur.

India then waited for 24 years. Reasons: sanctions, cost, and a hope that global disarmament would come. Pakistan's covert programme under A.Q. Khan and Chinese help to it changed the calculation.

cards.h: Pokhran-II (1998): becoming a nuclear weapon state
cards.b:
On 11 and 13 May 1998, under Vajpayee, India tested five devices (Operation Shakti), including a thermonuclear device. Vajpayee wrote to President Clinton citing China as the main threat. Pakistan tested at Chagai on 28 and 30 May.

The UNSC passed Resolution 1172 (June 1998) condemning the tests. The US and Japan imposed sanctions. India announced a voluntary moratorium on testing and began the Jaswant Singh–Strobe Talbott dialogue, which led over time to the 2005–08 nuclear deal.

K. Subrahmanyam, the father of Indian strategic thinking, had long argued for an open deterrent.

The National Security Advisory Board released a Draft Nuclear Doctrine in August 1999. The Cabinet Committee on Security adopted the official version on 4 January 2003.

  • Credible minimum deterrence.
  • No first use (NFU): nuclear weapons only in retaliation against a nuclear attack on Indian territory or forces anywhere.
  • Massive retaliation to inflict unacceptable damage.
  • Exception: India keeps the option of a nuclear response to a major attack with biological or chemical weapons.
  • No use against non-nuclear states.
  • Civilian control: the Nuclear Command Authority, with a Political Council chaired by the PM and an Executive Council chaired by the NSA. The Strategic Forces Command manages the arsenal.
  • Continued moratorium on tests, strict export controls, and support for a global, verifiable disarmament.

• Land: the Prithvi and Agni series. Agni-V (over 5,000 km). In March 2024 Mission Divyastra tested Agni-V with MIRV (multiple warheads).
  • Air: nuclear-capable fighter aircraft.
  • Sea: INS Arihant, a nuclear-powered ballistic missile submarine, was commissioned in 2016 and completed its first deterrence patrol in November 2018, completing the triad. INS Arighaat followed in 2024.

A sea-based force gives a secure second strike, which is essential for a no-first-use doctrine.

cards.h: Should India drop no first use?
cards.b: In 2019 Defence Minister Rajnath Singh said that NFU stands, but what happens in future depends on circumstances. Critics such as Bharat Karnad (Nuclear Weapons and Indian Security, 2002) want a bigger arsenal. Supporters of NFU say it has served India well.

In May 2025 India struck targets in Pakistan below the nuclear threshold. In his address on 12 May 2025 Modi said India would not tolerate nuclear blackmail. This shows the logic of the stability-instability paradox: limited conventional war under a nuclear umbrella.

Civil side: the SHANTI Act (December 2025) replaced the Atomic Energy Act, 1962 and the Civil Liability for Nuclear Damage Act, 2010, opening nuclear power to private companies under licence. The target is 100 GW of nuclear power by 2047. See the next lesson for the treaties.
